title: Texas data centers, 10 days of posts

clusters.text: Constellation Energy operates the largest nuclear fleet in America.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Constellation's FY2025 Form 10-K, filed with the SEC, says 
it is the largest nuclear energy company in the U.S.
. A 2026 Constellation 8-K repeats the same description. Independent outlets agree. Power Magazine and NucNet both describe it as holding or operating the largest US nuclear fleet. A September 2026 Motley Fool piece puts its nuclear capacity at 
about 22 GW, with the next-closest operators, Duke Energy and Vistra, at roughly 11 GW and 6.6 GW
. The Calpine acquisition completed in January 2026 added gas and geothermal capacity, not nuclear, so it does not change the ranking. The claim is accurate as worded. It has no bearing on Abbott's data-center freeze, but the claim does not assert any such link. Most of the supporting sources are the company's own filings and commentary, but the capacity comparison is consistent across them.

clusters.text: Data centers fund Ken Paxton's campaign and receive tax breaks from Texas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
NOTUS reviewed FEC reports and found that 
through June, Paxton's federal political operation had received at least $448,000 from executives and political committees of companies building, operating and investing in data centers
. KERA, the San Antonio Current and others repeated the finding. The money came from industry executives and PACs, not from data center facilities as such. It is also small next to the roughly 
$9.3 million raised by Paxton's war chest as of June 30
. On the tax side, Texas exempts qualifying data centers from state sales tax. The Texas Tribune reports 
Texas is forgoing at least $1.3 billion this year
, and a KXAN report on a Senate Finance hearing says the exemptions 
could cost the state $3.3 billion in forgone taxes by the 2028-29 budget cycle
. Both halves hold up, but the claim implies a link between the donations and the tax breaks that the sources don't establish. Paxton is not shown to have created or controlled the exemption. The Talarico campaign says he voted for the tax breaks, but I did not verify that vote.

clusters.text: The Texas grid's queue of large new loads, mostly data centers, reached 474 GW, up from 63 GW at the end of 2024 and more than five times record demand.
clusters.verdict_basis:
ERCOT's July 29, 2026 Senate presentation says it is tracking about 474 GW of large loads seeking interconnection as of June 2026, and about 90% of that is data centers. 
POWER magazine's reading of the chart puts the figure at roughly 474.7 GW, with 420.8 GW identified as data centers.
 The 63 GW baseline comes from ERCOT's December 2025 board materials, which compare 
about 226 GW of large loads seeking interconnection with 63 GW in December 2024
. The "five times record demand" comparison is Gov. Abbott's own wording in his Aug. 3 letter, and 
it refers to an all-time ERCOT hourly peak of 91,089 MW set on July 22, 2026
. 474 GW is about 5.2 times that peak. One caveat is that these are requests in the queue, many of them speculative, and not committed demand. The claim does say "queue," so it is worded accurately.

clusters.text: Texas has frozen new data center permits and grid hookups of 75 MW or more, and paused its big grid study.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim is largely accurate. On Sept. 21, 2026, 
Gov. Abbott ordered a halt to all data center permits sought from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality until the PUC and ERCOT finish the audit he started in early August
 (Sidley; CNBC). ERCOT's September Batch Zero update says it 
issued a Market Notice on Aug. 3 pausing the Batch Zero study process and paused approvals to energize data centers or crypto facilities of 75 MW or more
. Batch Zero is ERCOT's large-load interconnection study, so "big grid study" fits. Reporting adds that the pause 
covers only grid connections for data centers requesting at least 75 MW, and excludes smaller projects and those building their own power plants
 (Houston Public Media).

Two caveats: the 75 MW threshold belongs to the grid-hookup pause, not the permit freeze, which covers all data center permits. Both measures are pauses by gubernatorial directive pending the audit, and ERCOT's reports are due Dec. 10, 2026. The wording "frozen" and "paused" fits that, but it is not a permanent ban.

clusters.text: Only 9.5 GW of queued data center load is approved and about 4.3 GW is running; the rest is duplicates and speculation.
clusters.verdict_basis:
ERCOT's own reporting puts the approved figure close to the claim, but the "running" figure and the "duplicates and speculation" label don't match the record. ERCOT's June 2026 Monthly Operational Overview reports 8,926 MW with Approval to Energize. Of that, 
ERCOT observed a non-simultaneous monthly peak consumption of 3,966 MW in June 2026
. A secondary tracker cites a later ERCOT overview (Sept. 16) giving 9,456 MW approved, so "9.5 GW approved" is roughly right. I found no ERCOT figure of about 4.3 GW operating. The official operating numbers are about 3.9–4.0 GW, and ERCOT's earlier "observed energized" figure was higher (5,778 MW in the March 26 status data, per Corley Energy). The rest of the queue, about 474 GW of requests as of June 2026, is not characterized by ERCOT as duplicates or speculation. ERCOT's March 2026 data classify most of it as requests with no studies submitted (71.5%), under ERCOT review (21.1%), or with planning studies approved (5.2%). Reporting does say the queue is requests, not projects, and some may never be built (see the TokenPost and Data Center Frontier articles). Analysts do expect much of it to fall away. clusters.text: Data centers gave Ken Paxton's campaign about $450,000 to half a million dollars.
clusters.verdict_basis:
NOTUS reviewed FEC filings and found that, 
through June, Paxton's federal political operation received at least $448,000 from executives and political committees of companies building, operating and investing in data centers
. That figure covers several committees: 
his campaign, leadership PAC, joint fundraising committees and a pro-Paxton super PAC called Lone Star Liberty PAC
. So the roughly $450,000 figure is real, and outlets such as the 
San Antonio Current
, KERA and the Houston Chronicle repeated it. The claim still differs from the records in three ways:
- The money came from executives and corporate PACs at data-center-linked firms, not from "data centers" themselves.
- It went to a network of committees, not just the campaign. One example is a joint fundraising committee that 
splits the money it receives among Paxton's Senate campaign, his leadership PAC and the National Republican Senatorial Committee
.
- The "to half a million dollars" upper bound has no source. NOTUS gives a floor ("at least") as of June, with no stated ceiling.

A narrower count gave a much lower number. Nexstar's review of several Paxton-linked PACs

clusters.text: Under Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas has higher taxes and more data centers.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The "more data centers" half is defensible. 
DCD reports that Texas is fast becoming a data center hotspot, with ERCOT weighing more than 474GW of connection requests.
 Abbott has also reversed course. 
The Dallas Morning News says he froze new grid connections in August.
 
In September he told TCEQ to withhold new air and water permits until ERCOT finishes its audit.
 The claim doesn't mention this, and it undercuts any implication that Abbott is adding data centers now. The "higher taxes" half is vague and depends on the measure. 
Texas Policy Research says total property tax levies rose from $66.5 billion in 2019 to $89.4 billion in 2025.
 
The same source says the 2026–27 budget spends about $51 billion to maintain and expand relief.
 
Abbott's office says the homestead exemption rose from $15,000 to $140,000.
 
The Tax Foundation ranks Texas seventh in overall tax competitiveness, partly because it has no personal income tax.
 
The state ranks 38th in property tax competitiveness.
 The claim doesn't say what it is comparing taxes to (earlier years, other states, or rates versus bills). It also doesn't connect data centers to taxes. The tax record on data centers actually point

clusters.text: Vistra supplies nuclear and gas power in Texas amid the data center boom.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Vistra owns and operates the 2.4-GW Comanche Peak nuclear plant in Texas. 
DCD describes it as operated by Luminant Generation, a Vistra subsidiary.
 Vistra's SEC-reported deal, covered by Power Engineering, is 
a 20-year agreement to supply 1,200 MW from Comanche Peak
, and 
Utility Dive reports that Amazon is building a $5 billion data center near the plant
. On gas, Vistra's own release says it is 
building two new gas units totalling 860 MW at its Permian Basin plant
. It also describes 
upgrades that added more than 400 MW across its existing Texas gas fleet
. Reporting links Vistra's nuclear and gas sales to data-center demand, and Utility Dive adds that 
Vistra supports the Texas data center pause pending a review of the ERCOT queue
. The claim is accurate as worded. Comanche Peak power is contracted to begin delivery in late 2027, but Vistra's existing Texas fleet already supplies nuclear and gas power to the grid.

clusters.text: Ken Paxton gave data centers billions of dollars in special tax breaks.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The data center sales tax exemption is real and costs billions. The Texas Tribune reports that 
Texas will lose $3.2 billion in sales tax revenue over two years from the exemption, per the comptroller's office
. The Senate Finance Committee hearing put the projected cost at 
$3.3 billion in forgone taxes in the 2028-29 budget cycle
. But the records attribute the break to the Legislature, not Paxton. 
The Legislature passed House Bill 1223 in 2013
, and 
lawmakers expanded the incentive to larger data centers in 2015
. Paxton is the Attorney General and the Republican Senate nominee. He doesn't grant or certify tax exemptions, and nothing I found shows him doing so. CBS News reports that 
he wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers
. The only Paxton link in the results is a Talarico campaign spokesperson's allegation, reported by Fox News, that he 
took nearly half a million dollars from data center companies
. That is a campaign-money claim, not evidence that he gave anyone a tax break, so the claim wrongly attributes the action to him.

clusters.text: Oracle is trucking natural gas to power its AI data centers to avoid pipeline delays, including in Utah and Texas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Bloomberg reported on Oct 8, 2026 that Oracle has trucked compressed natural gas to data center sites while waiting for pipelines. 
The deliveries kept a data center outside Salt Lake City running for more than a year, according to people familiar with the work. Oracle also used trucked gas for initial work at its OpenAI campus in Shackelford County, Texas.
 I did not find Bloomberg's original article, so this rests on secondary coverage of it from Yahoo Finance, Data Center Dynamics, Trucking/TT News and others, which all describe the same report. 
The suppliers named were Certarus (Utah) and VoltaGrid (Texas).
 The report relies on unnamed sources, and I found no Oracle statement confirming it. The Texas use is described as early-stage work, and the Utah site was not named. The claim is accurate on its wording, including the stated purpose of avoiding pipeline delays. The Abbott freeze is background context and does not change the accuracy of the claim.

lanes.label: AI power boom is an opportunity

clusters.text: Trucked natural gas costs roughly four times as much as pipeline gas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim matches Bloomberg's reporting on Oracle trucking compressed natural gas to data centers, including the OpenAI campus in Shackelford County, Texas. Bloomberg cited Jack Weixel, an East Daley Analytics energy analyst. Secondary outlets (
Quartz
, 
SupplyChainBrain
) report his estimate that, once labor, equipment and fuel are counted, delivered CNG costs roughly four times the price of gas at a major pipeline hub. Two caveats: the figure is one analyst's estimate, not an audited or regulatory number, and it compares delivered trucked gas with hub prices rather than with every pipeline-delivered price. I could not retrieve the original Bloomberg article, so the sourcing rests on these secondary reports. The "roughly four times" wording is faithful to the reporting, and the reporting is about compressed gas specifically, not all trucked gas.

lanes.label: AI power boom is an opportunity

clusters.text: China is rapidly building data centers while the US fights over their construction.
clusters.verdict_basis: CNN's 13 October 2026 report is headlined "The US is fighting over data centers. China is building them fast." It reports that Beijing announced a $560 billion plan to scale up computing infrastructure and that Ulanqab's data center park took shape in about two years. SemiAnalysis likewise estimates China has over 24 GW of capacity and routinely delivers 100 MW facilities in under 12 months, with permitting taking 3–6 months against 12–13 months in the US. The US side is also documented. Dallas News, NBC DFW and Foley report that Gov. Abbott froze new grid connections in August and ordered TCEQ on 21 September to halt all data center permits, amid public opposition and an election-year dispute. The claim's wording is loose and leaves out that the US still has far more AI data centers (about 10 times China's, per CNN citing Stanford). US firms are also still investing much more (about $800 billion, against roughly $139 billion from listed Chinese companies), so the fight is over pace and siting, not an absence of building. That context does not contradict the claim as worded.

lanes.label: AI power boom is an opportunity

clusters.text: Power and AI infrastructure stocks have dropped sharply recently because of macro conditions and the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The drop is real, and macro conditions are well documented as a cause. 
Stocks fell on Oct. 14 after a hotter-than-expected inflation report
, and 
Reuters reported that prospects of higher interest rates intensified concerns over financing the AI buildout
. CNN and Reuters also pointed to non-macro drivers, including 
a Chinese memory-chip announcement
 and 
a Barclays downgrade of Dell and HPE
. Those pieces mostly cover chips, neoclouds and server makers, not power stocks. For Texas power names, a Sept. 14 TIKR analysis tied Vistra's slide to 
ERCOT forward power prices for 2027
. Abbott's data center freeze also matters, since 
his order widened an August freeze on new grid connections
. I found no reporting that says the midterms caused the selloff. The midterms appear as a forward-looking risk: 
CNBC says equity markets and politics could be on a collision course in November
, and 
AP-syndicated reporting says the data center backlash is spilling onto Wall Street
. Because the claim states a two-part cause as settled fact, and the midterm half rests on analyst concern rather than a documented driver of the drop, it is misleading.
